questions.question: Controlled vs uncontrolled inputs — how do they work, and when is each the right choice?
questions.title: Controlled Vs Uncontrolled
questions.direct_answer: CONTROLLED: React state is the single source of truth — value={state} + onChange={setState} on every keystroke; the input displays whatever state says (typing goes through React: change → state update → re-render → input shows the new value). Full control: instant validation, conditional disabling, formatting-as-you-type, and the form is always a valid JS object. UNCONTROLLED: the DOM owns the value — the input is rendered with a defaultValue and reads via a ref (inputRef.current.value) at submit time; keystrokes never round-trip through React. Cheaper renders, natural typing speed, and required for the cases where the DOM must win (large forms, file inputs, integrating non-React widgets).

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why the controlled/uncontrolled warning exists (the mechanism): React's input handling branches on which props you pass — if value is set (even to undefined on a later render!) the input is controlled; if value is absent it's uncontrolled. An input that flips modes across renders hits the branch differently each time: a controlled render IGNORES DOM state changes, an uncontrolled render uses them — so the same user action produces different results per render, which React flags as a warning because the behavior is genuinely unpredictable. The classic trigger is value={maybeUndefined} — fix it with value={x ?? ''} so the prop is always a real string.

The performance nuance behind 'uncontrolled is faster' (the honest numbers): the per-keystroke cost of controlled inputs is ONE re-render of the form subtree — for a typical form with 10 inputs that's trivially cheap. It becomes a real issue at scale: a 200-field form, or a value that drives expensive derived work per character (a search that filters 10k rows synchronously on each keystroke). The fixes in order: memoize the expensive consumer (not the input), debounce the derived work while keeping the input controlled for snappiness, and only then go uncontrolled with refs. The classic pattern from the docs: controlled for the feel + debounce for the cost.

The library reconciliation (worth naming): react-hook-form is uncontrolled BY DESIGN — it registers refs and reads at submit, which is why it re-renders ~zero times per keystroke (only the specific field's error state update) and why it scales to huge forms; it uses Controller as the escape hatch to wrap controlled components (design-system inputs that only accept value props). Formik is the controlled-state classic (form state in a single object, re-renders on each keystroke). Knowing this explains library choice from first principles: per-field subscriptions (uncontrolled refs) vs whole-form state (controlled) is exactly the trade you just described.
